name: Utility Tree
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Turning Vague Goals Into Testable Scenarios: The Utility Tree
lesson.summary: A utility tree is an architecture evaluation technique that breaks a vague goal like 'the system should be reliable' down into concrete, rankable scenarios, giving teams a structured way to decide which quality attributes deserve the most engineering effort.
lesson.body:
Telling an engineering team that a system should be secure, fast, and easy to change is not useful guidance. It is a wish list, and every architect on the team will silently interpret those words differently. The utility tree is a technique from architecture evaluation practice, used alongside methods like the Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method, designed specifically to solve this problem by forcing vague goals into a form specific enough to test, prioritize, and disagree about productively.

The tree has a simple shape. The root is labeled utility, standing in for overall system goodness. The first level of branches are the quality attributes from the previous section: performance, security, modifiability, reliability, and whatever others matter for the project. Each of those branches splits further into more specific refinements, and the leaves at the bottom are individual scenarios, concrete statements of a stimulus, a response, and a measurable outcome. Each leaf then gets two ratings, typically high, medium, or low: how important this scenario is to the business, and how difficult or risky it will be for the architecture to satisfy.

This is exactly where quality attribute and business requirement meet in practice. A quality attribute on its own is an abstract category. A business requirement on its own is often stated in terms too vague to build against. The utility tree is the mechanism that operationalizes the first using the second, turning "the system should be reliable" into a leaf that a stakeholder, not just an engineer, has actually agreed matters and has actually agreed is important enough to prioritize.

Consider building a small utility tree for a stablecoin payment network. Under the performance branch, a leaf might read, the system processes 1,000 transactions per second at peak load with 95th percentile confirmation under two seconds, rated high importance and high difficulty, because payment volume is the whole product and current consensus designs strain under that load. Under the security branch, a leaf might read, the cost of mounting a 51 percent attack exceeds 500 million dollars, rated high importance but lower difficulty if the chosen consensus mechanism already makes that true by design. Under modifiability, a leaf might read, a new token type can be added without a hard fork, rated only medium importance for a network focused narrowly on one stablecoin.

The value of writing all this out is not the diagram itself, it is the sorting that follows. Scenarios rated high importance and high difficulty are exactly where architectural attention should concentrate first, because they represent the goals that matter most and are least likely to happen by accident. Scenarios rated low importance, regardless of how loudly one engineer argues for them, can reasonably wait. Without this discipline, teams tend to spend their scarce engineering time on whatever quality attribute the most persuasive or most recently frustrated person in the room happened to complain about, which is rarely the same thing as what the business, and its stakeholders, actually need most.
